- It is stored only if the sending unit of work commits; a time in the past is due at once.
- `cancel` returns `false` when the command is already being delivered, was handled, was cancelled, or is unknown.
- Unlike a deadline, a scheduled command is not cancelled when the saga ends: cancel it yourself if it must not run.
- From a saga step, its `CommandId` is saga-scoped, and a final failure is reported to the saga like any outbox
  command's.

## What it needs

- **An `IN_TRANSACTION` outbox that can schedule messages**: the in-memory transport over the Postgres message store
  (the Spring Boot starter's default setup). With the default `ImmediateDispatchOutbox`, a saga that declares a deadline
  fails startup, and `schedule` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`.
- **Not with Spring Modulith interop**: Modulith's publication registry has no due time. When a saga declares a
  deadline and `saga-forge.transport.modulith-interop` is not set, the starter keeps Saga Forge's own log beside
  Modulith's registry (and logs `saga.transport.modulithInterop.skipped`); an explicit `true` refuses to start.
- **One clock**: the runtime and the transport read the same `java.time.Clock` (in Spring Boot, a `Clock` bean, or
  the UTC system clock).
- **Postgres**: an existing database needs schema version V3, which `initialize-schema=migrate` applies (see
  [Database schema](schema.md)); without Flyway, apply `schema-upgrade-017.sql` (see
  [Operations](operations.md#schema-and-upgrades)).

## Timing

- A due message is picked up on the relay's next poll, so a deadline runs up to `saga-forge.transport.poll-interval`
  after its due time, later if the relay is busy.
- Deadlines that came due while the application was down run once it is back. Each runs at most once; overdue
  messages are delivered in the order they were stored, not strictly in due order.
- A deadline the relay has already leased when the awaited event cancels it is still delivered, and ignored.
- With several application instances, a deadline is delivered once, by whichever instance's relay leads when it
  comes due; one started or cancelled on any instance behaves the same. During a takeover after a crash it can run up
  to `saga-forge.transport.leadership.lease-duration + check-interval` late (see
  [Running several instances](operations.md#running-several-instances)).

## Testing

`SagaFixture` moves its clock with `whenTimeElapses(Duration)` or `whenTimeReaches(Instant)` and then delivers
everything due, earliest first. `when(event)` never delivers merely-due messages:

```java
    @Test
    @DisplayName("an abandoned card challenge: the window closes, the stock is released and the order rejected")
    void abandonedChallengeTimesOut() {
        fixture.given(PLACED, RESERVED)
                .whenTimeElapses(Duration.ofMinutes(29))
                .expectNoCommands();

        fixture.whenTimeElapses(Duration.ofMinutes(1))
                .expectDeadlineExpired("paymentWindow")
                .expectCompensations("cancelCheckout")
                .expectCommands(new RejectOrderCommand("o-1", Order.RejectionReason.PAYMENT_TIMED_OUT),
                        new ReleaseStockCommand("o-1"))
                .expectCompensatedAfter("onPaymentWindowExpired")
                .expectStatus(SagaStatus.COMPENSATED)
                .expectOutcomeEvent(SagaCompensated.class, compensated ->
                        compensated.trigger().kind() == CompensationTriggerKind.DEADLINE_EXPIRED
                                && "paymentWindow".equals(compensated.trigger().deadlineName()));
    }
```

Source: `saga-forge-example/src/test/java/io/github/gkosharovdev/sagaforge/example/checkout/CheckoutSagaFixtureTest.java`.

More in [Testing](testing.md#deadlines): `expectOpenDeadline`, `expectNoOpenDeadline`, `expectDeadlineIgnored`,
`InstanceView.openDeadlines()` and `Builder.property(key, value)` for `${key}` durations.

<!-- docs/guide/vocabularies.md -->

# Vocabularies: a jMolecules domain

Saga Forge reads the domain side of a model (aggregates, their identifiers, domain events, commands and command
handlers) through *vocabularies* of markers. Its own annotations are always one. The `saga-forge-jmolecules` module
adds a second, so a domain marked only with [jMolecules](https://github.com/xmolecules/jmolecules) drives sagas with no
Saga Forge annotation on it. The saga class itself keeps Saga Forge's annotations (`@Saga`, `@SagaStep`,
`@StartSaga`, `@EndSaga`, `@StartCompensation`, `@SagaCompensation`).

## Enable it

Add the module. With the Spring Boot starter nothing else is needed: the starter adds the vocabulary while
`saga-forge.jmolecules.enabled` is not `false`.

```xml
        <dependency>
            <groupId>io.github.gkosharovdev</groupId>
            <artifactId>saga-forge-jmolecules</artifactId>
            <version>${project.version}</version>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.jmolecules</groupId>
            <artifactId>jmolecules-events</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.jmolecules</groupId>
            <artifactId>jmolecules-cqrs-architecture</artifactId>
        </dependency>
```

Source: `saga-forge-example-jmolecules/pom.xml`.

`jmolecules-events` is needed for events, `jmolecules-cqrs-architecture` for commands and command handlers. Keep the
domain package in the scanned packages:

```properties
# The domain lives beside the application package; the starter scans it for jMolecules aggregates and handlers.
saga-forge.scan-packages=io.github.gkosharovdev.sagaforge.example.jmolecules.domain
```

Source: `saga-forge-example-jmolecules/src/main/resources/application.properties`.

A hand-assembled runtime passes one `DomainTypes` to the runtime and the transport (`SagaRuntime.Builder.domainTypes`,
`InMemoryTransport.Builder.domainTypes`); a fixture test passes it to `SagaFixture.Builder.domainTypes` (see
[Testing](testing.md#a-jmolecules-domain)). Saga Forge's annotations stay recognised, and a model may mix both.

## The domain

The aggregate implements `AggregateRoot<T, ID>`, so its identifier is `getId()`, and marks its handler with jMolecules'
`@CommandHandler`. Events and commands carry the order's typed identifier, which links them to the aggregate:

```java
public final class Order implements AggregateRoot<Order, OrderId> {
  // ...
  @CommandHandler
  public void handle(ReserveStock command) {
    if (inStock) {
      status = Status.COMPLETED;
      events.add(new OrderCompleted(id));
    } else {
      status = Status.OUT_OF_STOCK;
      events.add(new StockUnavailable(id));
    }
  }
  // ...
  /** The events recorded since the repository last took them, oldest first. */
  public List<Object> domainEvents() {
    return List.copyOf(events);
  }

  public void clearDomainEvents() {
    events.clear();
  }
}
```

Source: `saga-forge-example-jmolecules/src/main/java/io/github/gkosharovdev/sagaforge/example/jmolecules/domain/Order.java`.

```java
public record PaymentProcessed(OrderId orderId, String paymentId, BigDecimal amount)
    implements DomainEvent {}
```

```java
@Command
public record ReserveStock(OrderId orderId) {}
```

Source: `PaymentProcessed.java` and `ReserveStock.java` in the same package.

The saga is the canonical one, unchanged: `@SagaStep(associationProperty = "orderId")` reads the event's `orderId`
member, whatever its type.

## What is recognised

| Role | jMolecules marker | Identifier or link |
|---|---|---|
| aggregate | `@AggregateRoot`, `AggregateRoot<T, ID>` | the `@Identity` field or method; for `AggregateRoot<T, ID>` without one, `getId()` |
| domain event | `@DomainEvent`, `DomainEvent` | one link member, below |
| command | `@Command` (also the deprecated `cqrs.annotation.Command`) | at most one link member |
| command handler | `@CommandHandler` on a method or constructor | - |

A link member is a declared field or record component of type `Association<A, ID>`, one marked
`@Association(aggregateType = A.class)` or `@Association`, or one whose type implements jMolecules' `Identifier`.
Without a named aggregate, the link resolves to the one aggregate whose identifier has the member's type. A plain
`String` or `UUID` member is never a link. When two aggregates share an identifier type, validation names both: name
the aggregate on the link, or give each aggregate its own identifier type.

Not recognised: `@DomainEventHandler`, `@Repository`, `@Service`, and any saga-side marker.

### Typed identifiers

Associations, the in-memory transport's ordering keys and aggregate references use an identifier's text form
(`String.valueOf`). Keep it the plain value and the same in every event and command of a saga:

```java
public record OrderId(String value) implements Identifier {

  public OrderId {
    Objects.requireNonNull(value, "value");
  }

  @Override
  public String toString() {
    return value;
  }
}
```

Source: `saga-forge-example-jmolecules/src/main/java/io/github/gkosharovdev/sagaforge/example/jmolecules/domain/OrderId.java`.

Loaders, savers and Spring Data repositories receive the identifier value itself, not its text.

### Outbox commands

jMolecules has no delivery attribute. A command handled after the sender commits keeps Saga Forge's `@Command` beside
jMolecules' one:

```java
@org.jmolecules.architecture.cqrs.Command
@io.github.gkosharovdev.sagaforge.core.annotation.Command(delivery = CommandDelivery.OUTBOX)
record NotifyCustomer(OrderId orderId) {}
```

## Events held on the aggregate

A jMolecules aggregate usually holds its events instead of calling `DomainEvents.record`. Register an
`AggregateEventSource`: after each aggregate command handler, and before the aggregate is saved, the runtime asks the
first source that supports the aggregate's type for its events and records them, in order, as if the handler had
recorded them. They continue the saga in the same unit of work and roll back with it.

```java
@Component
public class OrderEventSource implements AggregateEventSource {

  @Override
  public boolean supports(Class<?> aggregateType) {
    return Order.class.isAssignableFrom(aggregateType);
  }

  @Override
  public List<Object> takeEvents(Object aggregate) {
    Order order = (Order) aggregate;
    List<Object> events = order.domainEvents();
    order.clearDomainEvents();
    return events;
  }
}
```

Source: `saga-forge-example-jmolecules/src/main/java/io/github/gkosharovdev/sagaforge/example/jmolecules/application/OrderEventSource.java`.

With the starter, define it as a bean (several are asked in `@Order` order); by hand, pass it to
`SagaRuntime.Builder.aggregateEventSource`; in a fixture test, to `SagaFixture.Builder.aggregateEventSource`. A source
must clear what it returns, or the next handler call on the same aggregate returns the events again. Every returned
object must be a domain event of an enabled vocabulary, otherwise the handling fails with
`Event source {S} returned {T} for aggregate {A}, which is not a domain event (accepted: ...)`.

A Spring Data aggregate with `@DomainEvents` and `@AfterDomainEventPublication` needs no source in a Spring Boot
application: its events are published when the repository saves it and reach sagas through the starter's inbound
route, like any event published through `ApplicationEventPublisher`. If you register a source for such an aggregate
anyway, it takes and clears the events before the save, so Spring Data publishes nothing for them and each event
reaches the saga once.

## Another vocabulary

A team with its own markers implements `DomainTypeResolver` (`core.spi.model`): it names the vocabulary, answers which
role a type has (`role`, or `roles` when one class could carry two), which members identify or link it
(`identifiers`), whether an executable is a command handler (`commandHandler`), and how its markers read in error
texts (`describe`, `describeIdentifier`). An empty answer means "this vocabulary does not mark it". With the starter,
define the resolver as a bean; by hand, pass `DomainTypes.of(resolver)` to the runtime, the transport and the fixture.
`saga-forge-jmolecules`' `JMoleculesDomainTypeResolver` is the worked example.

## Checking what is enabled

The `sagaforge` Actuator endpoint lists `vocabularies` (Saga Forge's first) and `eventSources` (class names, in the
order the runtime asks them). Error texts name the marker the model used, for example
`jMolecules @CommandHandler method handle in NoCommandHandler must declare exactly one command parameter (@Command, or jMolecules @Command), found 0`;
see [Validation rules](validation-rules.md#vocabularies-of-markers).

<!-- docs/guide/testing.md -->

# Testing with `SagaFixture`

`saga-forge-test` (test scope) runs a saga's given/when/then tests on the shipped `SagaRuntime` over in-memory parts:
routing by association, the unit of work, duplicates, retries and compensation behave as in production. No database,
transport or Spring context, no JUnit extension: a failed expectation throws `SagaExpectationError` (an
`AssertionError`). Public API: package `io.github.gkosharovdev.sagaforge.test`.

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.gkosharovdev</groupId>
    <artifactId>saga-forge-test</artifactId>
    <version>0.4.0</version>
    <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
```

## Record and answer (the saga's own logic)

By default no command handler runs. Each command a step sends is recorded and counts as handled; the test answers it by
publishing the event the handler would have recorded.

```java
class OrderProcessingSagaFixtureTest {

    private static final BigDecimal AMOUNT = new BigDecimal("10.00");

    @Test
    @DisplayName("happy path: the payment reserves the stock")
    void paymentReservesStock() {
        SagaFixture.of(OrderProcessingSaga.class).build()
                .given(new OrderCreatedEvent("o-1", AMOUNT))
                .when(new PaymentProcessedEvent("payment-1", "o-1", AMOUNT))
                .expectCommands(new ReserveStockCommand("o-1"))
                .expectContext("paymentId", "payment-1")
                .expectCompletedStep("processPayment")
                .expectStatus(SagaStatus.RUNNING)
                .expectNoOutcomeEvent();
    }

    @Test
    @DisplayName("compensation path: missing stock refunds the payment")
    void missingStockRefundsThePayment() {
        SagaFixture.of(OrderProcessingSaga.class).build()
                .given(new OrderCreatedEvent("o-2", AMOUNT), new PaymentProcessedEvent("payment-2", "o-2", AMOUNT))
                .when(new StockUnavailableEvent("o-2"))
                .expectCompensations("compensatePayment")
                .expectCommands(new RefundPaymentCommand("saga-1", "payment-2", AMOUNT))
                .expectCompensatedAfter("rejectOrder")
                .expectOutcomeEvent(SagaCompensated.class, compensated ->
                        compensated.trigger().kind() == CompensationTriggerKind.FAILURE_OUTCOME
                                && compensated.trigger().stepName().equals("rejectOrder"));
    }
}
```

Source: `saga-forge-example/src/test/java/io/github/gkosharovdev/sagaforge/example/OrderProcessingSagaFixtureTest.java`.

Given events run exactly like the event under test, but only what the event under test causes counts for the
expectations. A fixture is one scenario: a later `when` continues from the state the earlier ones reached. Saga ids
are `saga-1`, `saga-2`, ..., so command identities and commands carrying the saga id are predictable.

## Handler mode (handlers and aggregates run)

```java
class OrderSagaFixtureTest {

    private final PaymentProvider provider = new PaymentProvider();
    private final SagaFixture fixture = SagaFixture.of(OrderProcessingSaga.class, Order.class)
            .handlers(new PaymentService(provider))
            .build();

    @Test
    @DisplayName("an in-stock order is paid for and completed in one call")
    void completes() {
        BigDecimal amount = new BigDecimal("25.00");

        fixture.givenAggregates(Order.create("o-1", true))
                .when(new OrderCreatedEvent("o-1", amount))
                .expectCommands(new ProcessPaymentCommand("o-1", amount), new ReserveStockCommand("o-1"))
                .expectContext("orderAmount", "25.00")
                .expectEndedWith("completeOrder")
                .expectOutcomeEvent(SagaCompleted.class, completed -> completed.outcomeStep().equals("completeOrder"));

        assertThat(fixture.aggregate(Order.class, "o-1").orElseThrow().status()).isEqualTo(Order.Status.COMPLETED);
        assertThat(provider.charges()).containsValue(amount);
    }

    @Test
    @DisplayName("an out-of-stock order is refunded")
    void refunds() {
        fixture.givenAggregates(Order.create("o-2", false))
                .when(new OrderCreatedEvent("o-2", new BigDecimal("9.50")))
                .expectCompensations("compensatePayment")
                .expectCompensatedAfter("rejectOrder")
                .expectStatus(SagaStatus.COMPENSATED)
                .expectOutcomeEvent(SagaCompensated.class,
                        compensated -> compensated.trigger().stepName().equals("rejectOrder"));

        assertThat(provider.refunds()).containsValue(new BigDecimal("9.50"));
    }
}
```

Source: `saga-forge-example-spring/src/test/java/io/github/gkosharovdev/sagaforge/example/spring/OrderSagaFixtureTest.java`.
This tests the Spring application's saga with its own `@Service` built by hand: no Spring context.

- `SagaFixture.of(SagaClass.class, AggregateClass.class, ...)` registers the model classes.
- `handlers(...)` runs the `@CommandHandler`, `@AggregateLoader` and `@AggregateSaver` methods of the objects passed,
  and the handlers of registered `@Aggregate` classes. A command whose handler is not registered is only recorded.
- Aggregates without a loader/saver live in an in-memory store: seed with `givenAggregates(...)`, read with
  `fixture.aggregate(type, id)`.
- Sagas with constructor dependencies: `sagaObjects(MySaga.class, () -> new MySaga(collaborator))`.

## Retries and failures

```java
@Test
@DisplayName("retried payment: two provider timeouts, one charge, the same idempotency key")
void retriedPayment() {
    PaymentProvider provider = new PaymentProvider();
    provider.timeOutNext(2);
    SagaFixture fixture = SagaFixture.of(OrderProcessingSaga.class).handlers(new PaymentService(provider)).build();

    Then then = fixture.when(new OrderCreatedEvent("o-3", AMOUNT))
            .expectAttempts("handleOrderCreated", 3)
            .expectCommands(new ProcessPaymentCommand("o-3", AMOUNT), new ReserveStockCommand("o-3"));

    assertThat(then.result().allAttempts()).filteredOn(c -> c.command() instanceof ProcessPaymentCommand)
            .extracting(RecordedCommand::commandId).hasSize(3).containsOnly(then.result().commands().get(0)
                    .commandId());
    assertThat(provider.charges()).hasSize(1);
}
```

Source: `saga-forge-example/src/test/java/io/github/gkosharovdev/sagaforge/example/OrderProcessingSagaFixtureTest.java`.

- Retry waits advance `fixture.clock()` instead of sleeping.
- `failCommand(type, () -> exception)` fails every handling of a command type; add a count to fail the next n, or a
  predicate to match content. Failures are classified by the runtime's rules (`TransientFailure`, `FinalFailure`,
  `retryOn`).
- `result().commands()` holds the commands of the attempts that committed; `result().allAttempts()` every attempt.

### A failing outbox command

An outbox command that fails is treated as the in-memory transport treats it: a `FinalFailure` is given up on after one
attempt, any other failure after `outboxCommandAttempts(n)` attempts (default 1, the transport's `max-attempts` in
production). The saga that sent it then compensates in the same `when` step, and the outcome event's trigger has kind
`COMMAND_FAILED`.

```java
@Test
@DisplayName("a capture refused for good gives the stock back and cancels the order, as an impossible delivery does")
void refusedCaptureCancelsOrder() {
    SagaFixture refusing = SagaFixture.of(FulfilmentSaga.class)
            .register(LogisticsService.class, PaymentService.class, InventoryService.class)
            .failCommand(CapturePaymentCommand.class, AuthorizationExpired::new)
            .build();

    refusing.given(CONFIRMED)
            .when(new ShipmentDispatchedEvent("shipment-1", "o-1"))
            .expectCompensations("cancelOrder")
            .expectCommand(ReleasePaymentCommand.class, release -> release.paymentId().equals("payment-1"))
            .expectCommand(CancelOrderCommand.class, cancel -> cancel.orderId().equals("o-1"))
            .expectCompensatedAfter("onShipmentDispatched")
            .expectFailure(AuthorizationExpired.class, FailureClassification.FINAL)
            .expectOutcomeEvent(SagaCompensated.class, compensated ->
                    compensated.trigger().kind() == CompensationTriggerKind.COMMAND_FAILED
                            && CapturePaymentCommand.class.getName().equals(compensated.trigger().commandType()));
}
```

Source: `saga-forge-example/src/test/java/io/github/gkosharovdev/sagaforge/example/checkout/FulfilmentSagaFixtureTest.java`.

`result().outboxFailures()` still lists every failed attempt; `result().commands()` leaves out the failed command.

## Deadlines

The fixture's clock only moves when the test says so. `whenTimeElapses(Duration)` and `whenTimeReaches(Instant)` move
it, then deliver every deadline and scheduled command due by then, earliest first, until nothing is due.
`given(...).givenTimeElapses(...)` lets time pass in the history. `when(event)` delivers nothing that is merely due.

```java
    @Test
    @DisplayName("a dispatch in time stops the deadline; three hours later the saga still waits for the delivery")
    void dispatchInTimeStopsTheDeadline() {
        fixture.given(CONFIRMED)
                .when(new ShipmentDispatchedEvent("shipment-1", "o-1"))
                .expectNoOpenDeadline("courierAssignment");

        fixture.whenTimeElapses(Duration.ofHours(3)).expectNoCommands();
        assertThat(fixture.instance(FulfilmentSaga.class, "o-1").status()).isEqualTo(SagaStatus.RUNNING);
    }
```

Source: `saga-forge-example/src/test/java/io/github/gkosharovdev/sagaforge/example/checkout/FulfilmentSagaFixtureTest.java`.

- `Builder.property(key, value)` sets what a `${key:default}` duration reads:
  `SagaFixture.of(FulfilmentSaga.class).property("checkout.courier-assignment", "PT45M")`.
- `InstanceView.openDeadlines()` maps each open deadline's name to its id and due time.
- A timeout step that compensates shows `DEADLINE_EXPIRED` as the outcome event's trigger kind, with the deadline's
  name. [Deadlines](deadlines.md#testing) has the payment-window test.

## Expectations

| Method | Checks |
|---|---|
| `expectCommands(Object...)` | exactly these commands, in order (`equals`) |
| `expectCommandsMatching(Predicate...)` / `expectCommand(Class, Predicate)` / `expectNoCommands()` | commands by predicate / at least one match / none |
| `expectHandled()` / `expectUnhandled()` / `expectStarted()` | some / no instance handled the event / it started the instance |
| `expectOutcome(HandlingOutcome)` | `WAITING`, `COMPLETED`, `DUPLICATE`, `DUPLICATE_START`, `UNMATCHED`, ... |
| `expectCompletedStep(String)` / `expectAttempts(String, int)` | the step completed / how often its unit of work ran |
| `expectStatus(SagaStatus)` / `expectEndedWith(String)` / `expectCompensatedAfter(String)` | final status / `COMPLETED` at that `@EndSaga` / `COMPENSATED` after that trigger |
| `expectCompensations(String...)` | these compensations ran, in order |
| `expectFailure(Class, FailureClassification)` | the recorded failure |
| `expectContext(String, Object)` / `expectNoContext(String)` | a `SagaContext` value or its absence |
| `expectOutcomeEvent(Class, Predicate)` / `expectOutcomeEvent(Class)` / `expectNoOutcomeEvent()` | exactly one outcome event (`SagaCompleted`, `SagaFailed`, `SagaCompensated`) of that type matching / of that type / none |
| `expectOpenDeadline(String)` / `expectNoOpenDeadline(String)` | the deadline is open (started, neither expired nor cancelled), or not |
| `expectDeadlineExpired(String)` / `expectDeadlineIgnored(String)` | the deadline came due and its `@DeadlineExpired` step ran / came due but the instance no longer waited on it |
| `instance(Class, String)` | switch to the instance with that association value (several sagas reacting) |
| `result()` | the `EventResult`, for your own assertions |

## Outcome events

When a saga ends, the runtime records one outcome event: `SagaCompleted`, `SagaFailed` or `SagaCompensated`. The
fixture collects the ones the event under test caused; `expectOutcomeEvent` checks that exactly one was committed and
that it matches, and `expectNoOutcomeEvent` that the saga is still running.

```java
    @Test
    @DisplayName("completion: the order's completion ends the saga and announces SagaCompleted")
    void completionIsAnnounced() {
        SagaFixture.of(OrderProcessingSaga.class).build()
                .given(new OrderCreatedEvent("o-4", AMOUNT), new PaymentProcessedEvent("payment-4", "o-4", AMOUNT))
                .when(new OrderCompletedEvent("o-4"))
                .expectEndedWith("completeOrder")
                .expectOutcomeEvent(SagaCompleted.class, completed -> completed.outcomeStep().equals("completeOrder")
                        && completed.associations().get("orderId").equals("o-4"));
    }

    @Test
    @DisplayName("start-step failure: the payment keeps timing out, the saga fails and announces SagaFailed")
    void startFailureIsAnnounced() {
        PaymentProvider provider = new PaymentProvider();
        provider.timeOutNext(10);
        SagaFixture fixture = SagaFixture.of(OrderProcessingSaga.class).handlers(new PaymentService(provider)).build();

        fixture.when(new OrderCreatedEvent("o-5", AMOUNT))
                .expectStatus(SagaStatus.FAILED)
                .expectOutcomeEvent(SagaFailed.class, failed -> failed.failedStep().equals("handleOrderCreated")
                        && failed.classification() == FailureClassification.EXHAUSTED && failed.attempts() == 3);
    }
```

Source: `saga-forge-example/src/test/java/io/github/gkosharovdev/sagaforge/example/OrderProcessingSagaFixtureTest.java`.

With a chosen `instance(...)`, only that instance's outcome event counts. `result().outcomeEvents()` lists them for
your own assertions. Build the fixture with `outcomeEvents(false)` to match an application that switched them off.

## A jMolecules domain

A model marked with jMolecules (see [Vocabularies](vocabularies.md)) passes its `DomainTypes` to the builder, and an
aggregate that holds its events gets its `AggregateEventSource`, which takes effect where aggregate handlers run
(`handlers(...)` mode or `handleAggregates`):

```java
  private SagaFixture fixture() {
    return SagaFixture.of(OrderProcessingSaga.class, Order.class)
        .domainTypes(DomainTypes.of(new JMoleculesDomainTypeResolver()))
        .handlers(payments)
        .aggregateEventSource(new OrderEventSource())
        .build();
  }
```

Source: `saga-forge-example-jmolecules/src/test/java/io/github/gkosharovdev/sagaforge/example/jmolecules/OrderProcessingSagaFixtureTest.java`.

The fixture has no Spring, so events that Spring would publish (Spring Data `@DomainEvents` on save) do not reach the
saga in a fixture test: register an event source for such an aggregate in the test.

## What the fixture catches before production

- An invalid model fails `build()` with the same `SagaRuntimeStartupException` as production
  ([Validation rules](validation-rules.md)).
- A `SagaContext` value Postgres cannot store (a `BigDecimal`, say) fails the test at the step that wrote it, with
  `Store it as a String (for example amount.toPlainString())`.

## Gotchas

- One event at a time on the test thread: no concurrency, leases or cross-aggregate ordering, and a failing outbox
  command is delivered again at once, without the transport's backoff.
- In record mode, a saga that sends an `@Command(delivery = OUTBOX)` command needs the handler's class registered
  (`register(HandlerClass.class)`), or `build()` fails rule R23.
- A `Long` stays a `Long` in the fixture, while Postgres reads a small one back as `Integer`.
- Aggregates without a no-argument constructor are not copied by the in-memory store, so a rolled-back change to one
  stays visible.

The full API is in the [fixture README](../../saga-forge-test/README.md) and the
[Javadoc](https://javadoc.io/doc/io.github.gkosharovdev/saga-forge-test).

<!-- docs/guide/operations.md -->

# Operations

## Properties

All properties of the Spring Boot starter (your IDE completes them from its configuration metadata). The starter's
[README](../../saga-forge-spring-boot-starter/README.md) describes what each assembled piece is and how to replace it
with your own bean.

| Property | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `saga-forge.enabled` | `true` | Whether Saga Forge's auto-configuration is active. |
| `saga-forge.scan-packages` | none | Packages scanned for saga model classes in addition to the application's packages. |
| `saga-forge.storage.type` | detected | Which storage module to use when several are on the class path (`postgres`). |
| `saga-forge.storage.postgres.initialize-schema` | `never` | `migrate` applies Saga Forge's versioned migrations with Flyway; `validate` checks the schema and fails on a difference; `always` creates the tables in an empty database; `never` fails startup if they are missing. See [Database schema](schema.md). |
| `saga-forge.storage.postgres.migration.history-table` | `saga_forge_schema_history` | Saga Forge's own Flyway history table. |
| `saga-forge.storage.postgres.migration.baseline-version` | unset | The version an existing database without Saga Forge's history is at; replaces detection. |
| `saga-forge.runtime.max-total-retry-backoff` | `30s` | Longest total wait a step's `@RetryPolicy` may add up to; a longer policy fails startup. |
| `saga-forge.outcome-events.enabled` | `true` | Whether a saga that ends records an outcome event (`SagaCompleted`, `SagaFailed` or `SagaCompensated`) with its last unit of work. |
| `saga-forge.application-events.mode` | `in-transaction` | `in-transaction`: recorded events, and events published through `EventPublisher`, are published as Spring application events inside the transaction. `after-delivery` (deprecated, refused while the inbound route is on): published when the transport delivers them, after the commit. `none`: not published. |
| `saga-forge.application-events.inbound.enabled` | `true` | Whether events published through Spring's `ApplicationEventPublisher` (also Spring Data `@DomainEvents`) whose type a saga has a step for are stored for sagas, in the publishing transaction. |
| `saga-forge.transport.workers` | `4` | Delivery threads; messages of one aggregate always use the same one. |
| `saga-forge.transport.max-attempts` | `10` | Failed deliveries before a message is set aside for an operator; for an outbox command a saga sent, also the attempts before its saga is told it failed (`EXHAUSTED`) and compensates. A `FinalFailure` is never retried. |
| `saga-forge.transport.initial-backoff` | `1s` | Wait after a message's first failed delivery, doubled per further failure. |
| `saga-forge.transport.max-backoff` | `1m` | Longest wait between delivery attempts. |
| `saga-forge.transport.lease-duration` | `5m` | How long a leased message is reserved for this instance before another may take it. |
| `saga-forge.transport.poll-interval` | `500ms` | Longest wait between polls when nothing signals new messages. |
| `saga-forge.transport.lease-batch-size` | `100` | Most messages leased at once. |
| `saga-forge.transport.retention` | `7d` | How long consumed messages are kept. |
| `saga-forge.transport.retention-sweep-interval` | `1h` | How often consumed messages older than the retention are removed. |
| `saga-forge.transport.leadership.lease-duration` | `30s` | How long the delivering instance's leadership lasts without renewal; after a crash a standby takes over once it expires. |
| `saga-forge.transport.leadership.renew-interval` | `10s` | How often the delivering instance renews its leadership; shorter than the lease duration. |
| `saga-forge.transport.leadership.check-interval` | `5s` | How often a standby instance checks whether it can take over; shorter than the lease duration. |
| `saga-forge.transport.modulith-interop` | `true` | Whether the transport keeps its messages in Spring Modulith's registry when it is present; not set and a saga declares a deadline, Saga Forge's own log is kept. |
| `saga-forge.telemetry.enabled` | `true` | Whether the application's OpenTelemetry instance is handed to the runtime and the transport. |
| `saga-forge.telemetry.tracing.enabled` | `true` | Whether saga spans are recorded. |
| `saga-forge.telemetry.metrics.enabled` | `true` | Whether saga metrics are recorded. |
| `saga-forge.telemetry.record-association-values` | `false` | Record association values (an order id, say) on spans. |
| `saga-forge.telemetry.record-contents` | `false` | Record saga event and command contents (`toString`, at most 1,000 characters) on spans. |
| `saga-forge.telemetry.record-failure-messages` | `false` | Record failure messages and exception events on spans; the failure's type is always recorded. |
| `saga-forge.telemetry.instance-count-interval` | `30s` | How often the `saga_forge.instances` gauge recounts the sagas by status. |
| `saga-forge.recovery.enabled` | `true` | Whether the runtime runs recovery sweeps on its own. |
| `saga-forge.recovery.interval` | `1m` | The time between two sweeps. |
| `saga-forge.recovery.stall-age` | `5m` | How long a compensating saga stays untouched before a sweep resumes it. |
| `saga-forge.recovery.batch-size` | `100` | Most sagas of each kind one sweep handles (1 to 1,000). |
| `saga-forge.recovery.abandonment-age` | `15m` | How long a created saga with no completed step waits before a sweep handles it. |
| `saga-forge.recovery.abandoned-start-policy` | `report` | `report` logs and counts an abandoned start; `fail` ends it `FAILED`. |
| `saga-forge.operations.expose-context-values` | `false` | Whether the `sagas` endpoint shows a saga's context values; they may hold personal data. |


## Schema and upgrades

With Flyway, `initialize-schema=migrate` applies everything below for you, as versioned migrations: see
[Database schema](schema.md). The scripts stay for hosts that apply the DDL themselves:

- `saga-forge-storage-postgres` ships its DDL as classpath resources under
  `io/github/gkosharovdev/sagaforge/storage/postgres/`: `schema.sql` (the complete current schema) and
  `schema-upgrade-005.sql`, `-006.sql`, `-007.sql`, `-010.sql`, `-011.sql`, `-017.sql`, `-013.sql`, `-015.sql`.
- A **new database** gets `schema.sql` only, through your migration tool (Flyway/Liquibase) or, in development,
  `saga-forge.storage.postgres.initialize-schema=always`. The current `schema.sql` already contains every upgrade.
- The **upgrade scripts** bring a database created by an earlier schema forward, in order; each names the schema it
  applies to in its header comment. Run each once, in one transaction, while no runtime is running. Release notes list
  any new upgrade script.
- `schema-upgrade-011.sql` renames the status `REQUIRES_INTERVENTION` to `COMPENSATION_FAILED` and removes the
  history rows of the dropped `REQUIRES_INTERVENTION` kind. Code that reads statuses by name must use the new name.
- `schema-upgrade-017.sql` adds the message store's due time and the `CANCELLED` status, for deadlines and scheduled
  commands.
- `schema-upgrade-013.sql` (after `-017.sql`) creates the leadership table `saga_message_store_leader` and drops the
  heartbeat table `saga_message_store_consumer`. Stop every instance before applying it.
- `schema-upgrade-015.sql` (after `-013.sql`) adds an instance's `resolution` and `compensation_round`, the operator
  columns of `saga_lifecycle_history` and the indexes the instance listing and the recovery sweeps use.
- Without `migrate`, Saga Forge never alters existing tables. With `initialize-schema=never` (the default), startup
  fails if tables are missing, naming them; `validate` also fails on a missing or different column or constraint.

## Actuator

With `spring-boot-starter-actuator` on the classpath:

```properties
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,sagaforge
```

- `GET /actuator/sagaforge` (read-only) returns the message store's counts per status (capped at 1,000 each) and the
  age of the oldest unconsumed message:

  ```json
  { "counts": { "CANCELLED": 4, "CONSUMED": 120, "SET_ASIDE": 1, "UNCONSUMED": 3 }, "oldestUnconsumed": "PT2.5S",
    "leadership": { "role": "STANDBY", "relayId": "a91e…",
      "leader": { "holderId": "7f3c…", "holderHost": "orders-1", "fencingToken": 12,
                  "acquiredAt": "2026-11-26T09:00:00Z", "expiresAt": "2026-11-26T09:12:30Z" } } }
  ```

  `role` is this instance's (`ACTIVE` or `STANDBY`); `leader` is the leadership record as last seen, absent before
  any was seen.
- **Schema version**: with Postgres storage, the payload also has a `schema` object with the configured mode, the
  version in Saga Forge's history (with `migrate`) and the startup check's result:
  `"schema": { "mode": "migrate", "version": "V5 (saga operations)", "check": "PASSED", "failures": 0, "warnings": 0 }`.
  See [Database schema](schema.md).
- The `sagaforge` health contributor is `DOWN` with a `setAside` detail while any message waits for an operator (a
  delivery that failed `saga-forge.transport.max-attempts` times), `DEGRADED` while no instance has led the message
  store for longer than one leadership lease, and `UP` otherwise. Its details carry `role`, `fencingToken` and, on a
  standby, `leader` as `holderId@holderHost`. Spring Boot leaves `DEGRADED` out of the overall health unless you add
  it to `management.endpoint.health.status.order` (see [Running several instances](#running-several-instances)).
- Switch them off with `management.endpoint.sagaforge.enabled=false` and `management.health.sagaforge.enabled=false`.
- The `sagas` endpoint lists, shows and repairs saga instances; see [Operating saga instances](#operating-saga-instances).

## OpenTelemetry

The runtime and the in-memory transport instrument themselves with the OpenTelemetry API. Without an SDK nothing is
recorded. With Spring Boot, nothing to add if the application already traces with OpenTelemetry
(`spring-boot-starter-opentelemetry`, or Micrometer Tracing's `micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel`): the starter passes the
application's `OpenTelemetry` bean on. Each unit of work, step, command and compensation becomes a span in the trace of
the code that published the start event, also across the message store and restarts.

**Metrics** are recorded through OpenTelemetry's metrics API. Spring Boot exports them only when the application
defines an `SdkMeterProvider` bean with an exporter, for example with `opentelemetry-exporter-otlp`:

```java
@Bean
SdkMeterProvider sdkMeterProvider(Resource resource) {
    return SdkMeterProvider.builder().setResource(resource)
            .registerMetricReader(PeriodicMetricReader.builder(OtlpHttpMetricExporter.getDefault()).build())
            .build();
}
```

Source: `saga-forge-spring-boot-starter/README.md` ("With OpenTelemetry"). Without it, spans are exported and saga
metrics are dropped.

**Privacy**: spans carry saga types, step and command names, generated ids, outcomes and failure types. Association
values, contents and failure messages are recorded only when switched on (`saga-forge.telemetry.record-*`).

### Telemetry reference

Spans (instrumentation scope `io.github.gkosharovdev.sagaforge`):

| Span | Kind | One per | Attributes (always) | Details |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `saga_forge.handle` | internal | saga type and instance an event reaches | `saga_forge.saga.type`, `saga_forge.event.type`, `saga_forge.handling.outcome`, `saga_forge.saga.started`, `saga_forge.failure.classification`, `error.type` | `saga_forge.saga.id`; association value\*, content\* |
| `saga_forge.attempt` | internal | attempt of a unit of work | `saga_forge.saga.type`, `saga_forge.attempt.result`, `saga_forge.failure.classification`, `error.type` | `saga_forge.saga.id`, `saga_forge.unit_of_work.id`, `saga_forge.attempt.number` |
| `saga_forge.step` | internal | step run | `saga_forge.saga.type`, `saga_forge.step`, `error.type` | `saga_forge.saga.id` |
| `saga_forge.command` | internal | command handling | `saga_forge.command.type`, `saga_forge.command.delivery`, `saga_forge.command.result`, `error.type` | `saga_forge.command.id`, `saga_forge.step`, `saga_forge.saga.id`, content\* |
| `saga_forge.compensation` | internal | compensation | `saga_forge.saga.type`, `saga_forge.step`, `saga_forge.compensation.status`, `saga_forge.compensation.trigger` | `saga_forge.saga.id`, `saga_forge.unit_of_work.id` |
| `saga_forge.delivery` | consumer | message the transport delivers | `messaging.system`=`saga_forge.inmemory`, `messaging.operation.type`=`process`, `saga_forge.message.kind`, `saga_forge.payload.type`, `error.type` | `messaging.message.id`, `saga_forge.delivery.attempt`; a failed outbox command: `saga_forge.command.classification` (`final`, `transient`, `unclassified`), and `saga_forge.command.reported`=`true` once its saga was told |
| `saga_forge.event.ignored` | internal | event no saga type reacts to | `saga_forge.event.type` | content\* |
| `saga_forge.operation` | internal | repair | `saga_forge.saga.type`, `saga_forge.operation.action`, `saga_forge.operation.result` | `saga_forge.saga.id`, `saga_forge.operator` |

Events on `saga_forge.handle`: `saga_forge.saga.started`, `saga_forge.saga.ended` (`saga_forge.saga.outcome`),
`saga_forge.retry.scheduled` (`saga_forge.attempt.number`, `saga_forge.retry.wait` in ms),
`saga_forge.compensation.started`. A start step that adopted a stranded `CREATED` instance sets `saga_forge.start.recovered`=`true` on its `saga_forge.handle` span. When a transport reports a failed outbox command, the runtime's reaction has a
`saga_forge.handle` span of its own, with `saga_forge.command.type`, `saga_forge.compensation.trigger`=`COMMAND_FAILED`
and `saga_forge.failure.classification` (`FINAL` or `EXHAUSTED`), and `saga_forge.handling.outcome` `COMPENSATED`,
`COMPENSATION_FAILED` or `IGNORED`. \* off by default; failure messages (`saga_forge.failure.message` and exception
events) likewise.

Metrics:

| Metric | Instrument | Unit | Attributes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `saga_forge.handle.duration`, `.attempt.duration`, `.step.duration`, `.command.duration`, `.compensation.duration`, `.delivery.duration` | histogram | s | the span's low-cardinality attributes |
| `saga_forge.saga.started` | counter | — | `saga_forge.saga.type` |
| `saga_forge.saga.ended` | counter | — | `saga_forge.saga.type`, `saga_forge.saga.outcome` (`completed:<step>`, `failed`, `compensated`, `compensation_failed`) |
| `saga_forge.event.handled` | counter | — | `saga_forge.saga.type`, `saga_forge.handling.outcome` |
| `saga_forge.retry.scheduled`, `saga_forge.retry.exhausted` | counter | — | `saga_forge.saga.type`, `saga_forge.step` |
| `saga_forge.deadlines` | counter | — | `saga_forge.saga.type`, `saga_forge.deadline.name`, `saga_forge.deadline.event` (`started`, `cancelled`, `expired`, `ignored`) |
| `saga_forge.command.failures` | counter | — | `classification` (`final`, `exhausted`): outbox commands the transport gave up on and reported to their saga |
| `saga_forge.message_store.messages` | gauge | `{message}` | `saga_forge.message.status` |
| `saga_forge.message_store.oldest_unconsumed.age` | gauge | s | — |
| `saga_forge.relay.active` | gauge | — | 1 while this instance's relay leads its message store, else 0 |
| `saga_forge.relay.leadership_changes` | counter | — | `saga_forge.leadership.change` (`acquired`, `lost`, `released`) |
| `saga_forge.operations` | counter | — | `saga_forge.operation.action` (`resume-compensation`, `compensate`, `resolve`), `saga_forge.operation.result` (`APPLIED` or the reason it was not) |
| `saga_forge.recovery` | counter | — | `saga_forge.recovery.kind` (`compensation_resumed`, `start_reported`, `start_failed`, `error`) |
| `saga_forge.instances` | gauge | `{saga}` | `saga_forge.saga.status`, `saga_forge.resolved`; recounted every `saga-forge.telemetry.instance-count-interval` |

A deadline delivery's `saga_forge.handle` span carries `saga_forge.deadline.name`; a delivery span of a message with a
due time carries `saga_forge.message.not_before` on its first attempt. A deadline that arrives when its instance no
longer waits on it is logged at INFO as `saga.deadline.ignored` with `reason=NOT_RUNNING`, `NOT_OPEN` or `REPLACED`.

Runtime log lines written inside a unit of work carry `traceId=` and `spanId=`.

Example alerts, in PromQL, assuming the OpenTelemetry-to-Prometheus name translation (dots become underscores,
counters gain `_total`, units become suffixes):

```promql
# Sagas failing or failing to compensate, per saga type
sum by (saga_forge_saga_type) (rate(saga_forge_saga_ended_total{saga_forge_saga_outcome=~"failed|compensation_failed"}[5m])) > 0

# Compensations as a share of finished sagas
sum(rate(saga_forge_saga_ended_total{saga_forge_saga_outcome="compensated"}[15m]))
  / sum(rate(saga_forge_saga_ended_total[15m])) > 0.05

# Retries exhausted
sum by (saga_forge_saga_type, saga_forge_step) (increase(saga_forge_retry_exhausted_total[15m])) > 0

# Outbox commands that failed for good and made their saga compensate
sum by (classification) (increase(saga_forge_command_failures_total[15m])) > 0

# Messages set aside for an operator
saga_forge_message_store_messages{saga_forge_message_status="SET_ASIDE"} > 0

# Delivery falling behind
saga_forge_message_store_oldest_unconsumed_age_seconds > 60
```


## Running several instances

Any number of instances can run over one database. Every instance accepts requests, runs units of work and appends
messages; the transports elect one **active** relay that delivers every message, deadline and scheduled command, while
the others are **standby**.

| Event | What happens | Takeover |
|---|---|---|
| Graceful stop of the active instance | It finishes its in-flight deliveries and releases the leadership | within `check-interval` (5 s) |
| Crash, network partition or long pause | Its leadership expires; a standby acquires a newer fencing token, and the store refuses the old one's leases | within `lease-duration + check-interval` (35 s) |
| Database unreachable for the active instance | It stops leasing one `renew-interval` before its lease ends by its own clock | as for a crash |

Delivery stays at least once: a message the old leader held may be delivered again by the new one, so handlers pass
their `CommandId` on. Delivery throughput is that of one instance; partitioned delivery is not supported.

Log events (logger of the transport): `saga.transport.leadership.acquired` (INFO, with `relay`, `host`,
`fencingToken`, `previousHolder`), `saga.transport.leadership.released` (INFO), `saga.transport.leadership.lost`
(WARNING, `cause=renewRefused`, `trustExpired` or `fenced`, and `newHolder` when known) and
`saga.transport.leadership.checkFailed` (WARNING, the store could not be reached; the role does not change by itself).

To make a leaderless store show in the overall health:

```properties
management.endpoint.health.status.order=down,out-of-service,degraded,up,unknown
management.endpoint.health.status.http-mapping.degraded=200
```

Alert on `max(saga_forge.relay.active) == 0` across instances for longer than `lease-duration + check-interval`.

**Why one active relay.** One consumer keeps per-aggregate order and due times simple, and a leadership lease with a
fencing token keeps a paused or partitioned instance from delivering beside the new leader. The design and the prior
art behind it (Kubernetes leases, Kafka epochs, Axon token claims and others) are in the
[architecture notes](../architecture.md#how-other-frameworks-solved-the-same-problems).

## Outcome events

When a saga instance reaches a terminal status, the unit of work that writes the status also records one outcome
event (`io.github.gkosharovdev.sagaforge.core.outcome`):

| Status | Outcome event |
|---|---|
| `COMPLETED` | `SagaCompleted`, with the `@EndSaga` step that ended it |
| `FAILED` | `SagaFailed` with `phase() == STEP`: the failed step, its classification, cause type and attempts |
| `COMPENSATION_FAILED` | `SagaFailed` with `phase() == COMPENSATION`: the compensation that failed, plus `compensationTrigger()` |
| `COMPENSATED` | `SagaCompensated`, with `trigger()`: why compensation started |

Every outcome event carries the saga type, the saga id, the instance's associations and the time. It never carries a
failure message, a `SagaContext` value or a saga field. Its `eventId()` is `sagaId:STATUS` and is the same on every
delivery, so a listener that must act once deduplicates on it.

An outcome event is **not a domain event**: no saga step can take one (the model is rejected at startup), and the
runtime hands a delivered outcome event to no saga. Applications, policies and other modules listen for it.

How reliably it arrives depends on the outbox, like any event the unit of work records:

| Outbox | Stored | Delivered |
|---|---|---|
| In-memory transport (own log) | in the terminal write's transaction | at least once |
| In-memory transport, Spring Modulith interop | in Modulith's registry, same transaction | at least once |
| `ImmediateDispatchOutbox` (the default without a transport) | not stored; dispatched after commit | at most once |
| Saga test fixture | staged in the transaction, released on commit | exactly once, synchronous |

**Listening.** In Spring Boot, outcome events are published as application events by the same rule as recorded events
(`saga-forge.application-events.mode`): use `@TransactionalEventListener` or `@ApplicationModuleListener`, which run
after the commit and never for a rolled-back unit of work; see [recipe 6](recipes.md#6-reacting-to-how-a-saga-ended).
In a plain Java host, register a delivery callback on the in-memory transport; the starter's deprecated after-delivery
bridge does exactly that:

```java
public ApplicationEventBridge(InMemoryTransport transport, ApplicationEventPublisher publisher) {
    this.publisher = publisher;
    transport.onDelivered(this::publish);
}
```

Source: `saga-forge-spring-boot-starter/src/main/java/io/github/gkosharovdev/sagaforge/spring/transport/ApplicationEventBridge.java`.

The in-memory transport orders outcome events per instance (ordering key `saga:<sagaId>`).

**Switching them off.** `saga-forge.outcome-events.enabled=false`, `SagaRuntime.Builder.outcomeEvents(false)` or, in
tests, `SagaFixture.Builder.outcomeEvents(false)`.

**Failures of the outbox.** With an `IN_TRANSACTION` outbox (the in-memory transport), a failure to store the outcome
event rolls back the write it belongs to: for a failed saga, the `FAILED` status is then not written, the runtime logs
`saga.instance.failedNotRecorded` and the exception reaches the caller. With an `AFTER_COMMIT` outbox the status stays
written and the failure is listed in the handling result's `outboxFailures()`.

**Failure text.** Outcome events carry no failure message, but logs and spans can (spans only with
`saga-forge.telemetry.record-failure-messages=true`). Mask secrets in your logging backend (Logback `%replace`, Log4j2
`RegexReplacement`) and in the OpenTelemetry Collector (`redaction` or `transform` processor). The `saga_instance` and
lifecycle-history tables keep the raw message.

## Messages set aside

The in-memory transport sets a message aside with one of these reasons, visible in `MessageStoreQueries` and the
Actuator endpoint:

| Reason | When | Saga told? |
|---|---|---|
| `MAX_ATTEMPTS` | delivery failed `saga-forge.transport.max-attempts` times | for an outbox command a saga sent: yes, `EXHAUSTED` |
| `FINAL_FAILURE` | an outbox command's handler threw a `FinalFailure`; not retried | for a command a saga sent: yes, `FINAL` |
| `UNREADABLE: ...` | the payload could not be read back | for an outbox command a saga sent: yes, `FINAL` |

When the saga is told, the message is set aside in the same transaction as the saga's reaction; if the reaction fails,
the message stays and is delivered again after the backoff. A saga that had already ended or was already compensating
is not changed: the runtime logs `saga.command.failure.ignored` (WARNING, with `sagaType`, `sagaId`, `sender`,
`command`, `commandId`, `classification` and `reason`: `missing`, `terminal:<status>`, `compensating`,
`already-compensated`, `not-compensated`, `nothing-committed` or `unknown-sender`). Redelivering a set-aside command
after its saga compensated runs its handler again but does not compensate twice.

## Statuses an operator sees

| `SagaStatus` | Meaning | Action |
|---|---|---|
| `RUNNING` | committed, waiting for the next event | none; a saga waits indefinitely (no timeouts) |
| `COMPLETED` | ended at an `@EndSaga` step (the outcome is its name) | none |
| `COMPENSATING` | compensations are being run | resumes on the next event, or by a recovery sweep once it is untouched for `stall-age`; `resume-compensation` |
| `COMPENSATED` | all committed steps undone; the trigger says why (a `@StartCompensation` step, a step's `FINAL` or `EXHAUSTED` failure, or a failed outbox command, `COMMAND_FAILED`) | none |
| `FAILED` | an unclassified failure; committed effects stay in place | investigate, then `compensate` or `resolve`; no retry of the failed step yet |
| `COMPENSATION_FAILED` | a compensation failed; the instance shows what was and was not undone | fix the cause, then `resume-compensation`; or undo by hand and `resolve` |
| `CREATED` | created, first unit of work not finished (a crash at that moment strands it) | a redelivered start event adopts it; a sweep reports it after `abandonment-age`; `compensate` |

## Operating saga instances

Every runtime has an operations API, `SagaRuntime.operations()` (`SagaOperations`), and the starter exposes it as the
`sagas` Actuator endpoint. It finds instances, repairs one at a time and runs recovery sweeps.

### Finding instances

- `list(SagaInstanceQuery)` returns one page, oldest modified first, filtered by status, saga type and modification
  time, with a `PageCursor` for the next page (`limit` 1 to 500, 50 by default). Pages are read one by one, so an
  instance that changes between two pages may appear on both or neither.
- `find(sagaId)`, `findByAssociation(name, value)`, `history(sagaId)` (the lifecycle history, oldest first),
  `context(sagaId)` and `count(statuses)` (per status, plus the `FAILED` and `COMPENSATION_FAILED` sagas no operator
  has resolved).

### The three repairs

Each repair takes an `OperatorRequest` (who, and why; both required) and returns `RepairResult.Applied` with the
instance after the repair, or `RepairResult.NotApplied` with the reason (`NOT_FOUND`, `WRONG_STATUS`,
`ALREADY_RESOLVED`) and the status it found. A repair runs under the instance's lock and re-reads the instance first,
so two operators, or an operator and a sweep, never repair the same instance twice.

| Repair | Applies to | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `resumeCompensation` | `COMPENSATION_FAILED`, or `COMPENSATING` | starts a new compensation round: failed compensations run again, compensated ones do not; ends `COMPENSATED` (outcome event id `sagaId:COMPENSATED:r<round>`) or `COMPENSATION_FAILED` again |
| `compensate` | `CREATED`, `RUNNING`, `FAILED` | compensates every committed step, most recent first; the trigger is `OPERATOR_REQUEST` with the request |
| `markResolved` | `FAILED`, `COMPENSATION_FAILED` | records that the saga was handled by hand; the status stays, the unresolved counts drop |

Every repair writes a lifecycle entry (`COMPENSATION_RESUMED`, `COMPENSATION_STARTED` or `RESOLVED`) naming the
operator and the reason. A compensation that runs again must be safe to run again: pass its `CommandId` on as the
idempotency key.

In a fixture test, `whenOperator` runs a repair and delivers what it sent
(`saga-forge-example/src/test/java/io/github/gkosharovdev/sagaforge/example/OrderProcessingSagaOperationsFixtureTest.java`):

```java
    fixture
        .whenOperator(
            operations ->
                operations.resumeCompensation(
                    sagaId, new OperatorRequest("alice", "provider back, refund retried")))
        .instance(OrderProcessingSaga.class, "o-1")
        .expectStatus(SagaStatus.COMPENSATED)
        .expectCommands(new RefundPaymentCommand(sagaId, "payment-1", AMOUNT))
        .expectHistory(
            SagaLifecycleEventKind.COMPENSATION_FAILED,
            SagaLifecycleEventKind.COMPENSATION_RESUMED,
            SagaLifecycleEventKind.COMPENSATED)
        .expectOutcomeEvent(
            SagaCompensated.class,
            compensated -> compensated.eventId().equals(sagaId + ":COMPENSATED:r1"));
```

`Then.expectResolved()` and `expectNotResolved()` check a resolution.

### Recovery sweeps

With the starter, every application instance sweeps once a minute (`saga-forge.recovery.*`); a runtime assembled by
hand sweeps only with `SagaRuntime.Builder.recovery(RecoverySettings.enabledWithDefaults())`, and `recover()` runs one
sweep on demand. A sweep:

- resumes the compensation of a saga `COMPENSATING` and untouched for `stall-age` (an instance whose compensation was
  interrupted and that no event reaches);
- handles a saga still `CREATED` with no completed step after `abandonment-age` (its first unit of work never
  committed): with `abandoned-start-policy=report` (the default) it logs `saga.recovery.startAbandoned` once per
  process and counts it; with `fail` it ends it `FAILED`.

`report` is the default because a start ended `FAILED` no longer matches its start event: a redelivered start event
would then start a second saga. Left `CREATED`, the instance is adopted by a redelivered start event, which runs the
start step on it and records `START_RECOVERED`. Choose `fail` when the start event will not come again.

Sweeps on several instances are safe without leadership: each repair re-checks the instance under its lock. Each
sweep handles at most `batch-size` sagas of each kind; the rest wait for the next sweep.

### The `sagas` endpoint

```properties
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,sagaforge,sagas
```

- `GET /actuator/sagas?status=FAILED&status=COMPENSATION_FAILED&type=…&modifiedBefore=…&modifiedAfter=…&limit=50&cursor=…`
  returns one page, the `next` cursor and the counts per status. A bad parameter is a 400.
- `GET /actuator/sagas/{sagaId}` returns the instance and its history; 404 if unknown. The saga's business state is
  never shown, its context values only with `saga-forge.operations.expose-context-values=true`.
- `POST /actuator/sagas/{sagaId}/{action}` with `{"reason": "…"}`, where `action` is `resume-compensation`,
  `compensate` or `resolve`. The authenticated principal is the operator; without one the answer is 401. A repair
  that does not apply is a 409 with the reason and the status.

The write operation is off until `management.endpoint.sagas.access=unrestricted`. Only allow it behind Spring
Security, with a role for operators
(`saga-forge-example-spring/src/test/java/io/github/gkosharovdev/sagaforge/example/spring/SagasEndpointWebContainerTest.java`):

```java
    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain actuatorSecurity(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
      http.authorizeHttpRequests(
              requests ->
                  requests
                      .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/actuator/sagas/**")
                      .hasRole("OPERATOR")
                      .anyRequest()
                      .permitAll())
          .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())
          .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable());
      return http.build();
    }
```

The `sagaforge` health contributor carries `instances.compensationFailed` and `instances.failedUnresolved`; they never
change its status. Telemetry: a `saga_forge.operation` span and the `saga_forge.operations` counter per repair (action
and result), the `saga_forge.recovery` counter per sweep result, and the `saga_forge.instances` gauge per status.

<!-- docs/guide/schema.md -->

# Database schema

Saga Forge keeps its state in six Postgres tables: `saga_instance`, `saga_association`, `saga_context`,
`saga_lifecycle_history`, `saga_message_store` and `saga_message_store_leader`. Since 0.5.0,
`saga-forge-storage-postgres` ships them as **versioned Flyway migrations** with their own history table. You no longer
copy Saga Forge's DDL into your own migrations, and Saga Forge's version numbers never meet yours.

| Version | What it adds | First released in |
|---|---|---|
| V1 base schema | the six tables as of 0.1.0 (with the heartbeat table the relay used then) | 0.1.0 |
| V2 saga outcome events | renames `REQUIRES_INTERVENTION` to `COMPENSATION_FAILED` | 0.2.0 |
| V3 saga deadlines | the message store's due time and the `CANCELLED` status | 0.4.0 |
| V4 active standby relay | the leadership table; drops the heartbeat table | 0.4.0 |
| V5 saga operations | resolutions, compensation rounds, operator columns and indexes | 0.5.0 |

The migrations live at `classpath:io/github/gkosharovdev/sagaforge/storage/postgres/migration`, and Flyway records them
in `saga_forge_schema_history`. A released version is never changed: a later schema change is always a new version.

## Choose a mode

The starter's `saga-forge.storage.postgres.initialize-schema` decides what happens at startup:

| Mode | Writes to the database | Fails startup when | Use it for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `never` (default) | never | a Saga Forge table is missing | schemas someone else manages; differences are only logged |
| `always` | creates the tables from `schema.sql` in a database without them | only some tables exist | local development and tests |
| `validate` | never | the schema check finds a missing or different table, column or constraint | Liquibase or DBA-managed schemas |
| `migrate` | applies the missing versions under Saga Forge's history | Flyway is absent, the tables match no version, a version fails, or the check fails afterwards | production with Flyway |

Every mode except `always` on an empty database runs the **schema check**. It compares the database with the version
the jar expects, by meaning, not by text:

- tables, columns (type and `NOT NULL`), primary keys, unique constraints, foreign keys (with their `ON DELETE`) and
  check constraints must be there; any difference is a **failure**;
- a missing or different index is only a **warning**: the library works without it, more slowly;
- extra tables, columns, constraints and indexes are ignored, so you can add your own.

A failure lists every difference, one per line:

```text
Saga Forge's schema does not match V5 (saga operations): 1 failure, 0 warnings.
  FAILURE saga_context: column last_modified_at is missing (expected timestamp with time zone NOT NULL)
```

## `migrate`: Saga Forge's migrations beside your own

Add Flyway's core and Postgres modules (Spring Boot manages their versions; an application that uses Flyway already
has them):

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.flywaydb</groupId>
    <artifactId>flyway-core</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.flywaydb</groupId>
    <artifactId>flyway-database-postgresql</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

```properties
saga-forge.storage.postgres.initialize-schema=migrate
```

At startup, Spring Boot's own database initialisers run first: your Flyway migrations (`flyway_schema_history`),
Liquibase, `spring.sql.init`. Then Saga Forge runs its own Flyway instance on its own location and history table,
then checks the result, then starts the runtime. Your Flyway settings (`spring.flyway.*`) don't apply to it, and
`spring.flyway.enabled=false` doesn't stop it. Several instances starting at once are safe: Flyway's lock lets one
apply each version and the others find it applied.

Because your tables are already in the schema, Saga Forge's history starts with a baseline row at version 0, then
records V1 to V5:

```text
 version | description             | type
---------+-------------------------+----------
 0       | << Flyway Baseline >>   | BASELINE
 1       | base schema             | SQL
 ...
 5       | saga operations         | SQL
```

Never copy Saga Forge's migrations into your own migration location: the numbers would clash with yours, and each
upgrade of Saga Forge would mean copying again.

| Property | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `saga-forge.storage.postgres.migration.history-table` | `saga_forge_schema_history` | Saga Forge's Flyway history table. |
| `saga-forge.storage.postgres.migration.baseline-version` | unset | The version an existing database without Saga Forge's history is at; replaces detection. |

## Taking over an existing database

A database created before 0.5.0 (from `schema.sql`, the upgrade scripts, or your own copy of them in your migrations)
has Saga Forge's tables but no Saga Forge history. The first start with `migrate` detects which released version the
tables match, records it as the baseline, and applies only the later versions. Every row is kept; V2 renames
`REQUIRES_INTERVENTION` to `COMPENSATION_FAILED` and V4 drops the heartbeat table, as the upgrade scripts did. If your
own migrations created Saga Forge's tables, your history stays as it is.

If the tables match no released version, for example because a column was dropped or a constraint changed by hand,
startup fails before anything is written and names the closest version and the differences:

```text
Saga Forge's tables exist but match no released schema version. Closest: V4 (active standby relay). Saga Forge's
schema does not match V4 (active standby relay): 1 failure, 0 warnings.
  FAILURE saga_instance: column outcome is missing (expected text NULL)
```

Repair the listed differences, or set `saga-forge.storage.postgres.migration.baseline-version` to the version the
database is at: Saga Forge then applies the later versions and checks the result.

## `validate`: schemas you manage yourself

With Liquibase, or with a DBA who applies DDL by hand, apply `schema.sql` for a new database or the matching
`schema-upgrade-NNN.sql` scripts for an existing one (see [Operations](operations.md#schema-and-upgrades)), and set:

```properties
saga-forge.storage.postgres.initialize-schema=validate
```

Startup then fails on any missing or different table, column or constraint, listing each one, and logs a warning for a
missing index. It never writes and never creates a history table.

## Plain Java

Without the starter, run the same migrations with your own Flyway and check the result with
`PostgresSchemaValidator`:

```java
static void migrate(DataSource dataSource) {
  PostgresSchemaValidator validator = new PostgresSchemaValidator(dataSource);
  String history = PostgresSchema.DEFAULT_HISTORY_TABLE;

  // A database built from schema.sql and the upgrade scripts has Saga Forge's tables but no
  // history: record the version it is at as the baseline. Otherwise the baseline is 0, which
  // lets Flyway start beside the application's own tables.
  String baseline = "0";
  if (validator.appliedVersion(history).isEmpty()) {
    switch (validator.detectVersion()) {
      case SchemaDetection.Matched matched ->
          baseline = String.valueOf(matched.version().number());
      case SchemaDetection.Unmatched unmatched -> throw SagaSchemaException.unmatched(unmatched);
      case SchemaDetection.Empty empty -> {}
    }
  }

  Flyway.configure()
      .dataSource(dataSource)
      .locations(PostgresSchema.MIGRATION_LOCATION)
      .table(history)
      .placeholderReplacement(false)
      .baselineOnMigrate(true)
      .baselineVersion(baseline)
      .load()
      .migrate();

  SchemaValidationReport report = validator.validate();
  if (!report.passed()) {
    throw SagaSchemaException.failedCheck(report);
  }
}
```

Source: `saga-forge-storage-postgres/src/test/java/io/github/gkosharovdev/sagaforge/storage/postgres/PlainJavaMigrationExampleTest.java`.

`saga-forge-storage-postgres` does not depend on Flyway: add `flyway-core` and `flyway-database-postgresql` to your own
build.

## Rolling deploys

During a rolling deploy, instances of the old and the new release run against one database. The new release's first
instance applies the new version; the old instances keep running on it only if that version keeps the previous
release working. Each release's notes say whether its schema version does. When it doesn't, stop every instance
before deploying, as the notes say. With `migrate`, an older jar against a newer database starts: Flyway ignores
versions it doesn't know.

<!-- docs/guide/limitations.md -->

# Limitations to design around (0.4.0)

These are known limits of the current release, most important first for a Spring Boot monolith on Postgres and the
in-memory transport. Each has an id in the project's gap register (`.specify/memory/memory.md`), so you can follow its
status in later releases.

| # | Limitation | Design around it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **One delivering instance per database** (G-013-01, G-013-02). Several instances share the message store, but only the elected relay delivers: delivery throughput is that of one instance, and a message appended on a standby waits for the leader's next poll (up to `saga-forge.transport.poll-interval`). | Size the delivering instance for the whole message rate; keep handlers short. Spread load with the Kafka transport once it exists. |
| 2 | **An operator cannot retry a failed step** (G-015-01): a `FAILED` saga can only be compensated or marked resolved, since the runtime does not keep the event that triggered the step. Repairs act on one instance at a time (G-015-05) and run its compensations in the calling thread, so a long compensation holds the HTTP call (G-015-04). | Make steps whose failure you would want to retry mark it `TransientFailure` so `@RetryPolicy` retries it; keep compensations short; script bulk repairs over `SagaOperations.list`. |
| 3 | **Retry backoff is in-process** (G-005-01): capped (30 s total by default), and a waiting retry blocks the delivering thread and holds the instance (G-005-02). | Keep retry policies short; for a long wait use a deadline whose timeout step re-arms it, or a scheduled command (see [Deadlines](deadlines.md)). |
| 4 | **Deadlines and scheduled commands do not work with Spring Modulith interop** (G-017-01): the starter keeps Saga Forge's own log for a model with deadlines unless `saga-forge.transport.modulith-interop` is set. A deadline runs up to one poll interval late (G-017-04); overdue ones run in stored, not due, order after downtime (G-017-03). | Leave the interop property unset (or `false`) when a saga declares a deadline. Don't rely on sub-second deadline precision or on the order of two overdue deadlines. |
| 5 | **Two logs are not ordered against each other** (G-014-01): with Saga Forge's own log beside Modulith's registry, an aggregate's events in one log have no order against those in the other. Saga Forge's log orders its events per aggregate on every publishing route. | If you send an aggregate's events on to a broker, send them through one of the two, keyed by the aggregate id, and give consumers an aggregate version to drop stale events. |
| 6 | **An event published inside a host transaction waits for the relay's next poll** (G-014-05), up to `saga-forge.transport.poll-interval`, whether published through Spring or through `EventPublisher`. | Keep the poll interval short where saga start latency matters. |
| 7 | **An abandoned start is only reported by default** (`abandoned-start-policy=report`): a crash between creating an instance and its first unit of work leaves it `CREATED` until its start event is redelivered, which adopts it. The report is deduplicated per process, so each instance logs it again after a restart (G-015-07). | Alert on `saga.recovery.startAbandoned` or the `saga_forge.recovery{kind=start_reported}` counter; choose `fail` when the start event will not come again. |
| 8 | **Schema migrations need Flyway** (G-018-01): `initialize-schema=migrate` runs Saga Forge's versioned migrations with Flyway only; there are no Liquibase changesets. | With Liquibase or DBA-managed DDL, apply `schema.sql` and the upgrade scripts yourself and set `initialize-schema=validate` (see [Database schema](schema.md)). |
| 9 | **Saga metrics need an OpenTelemetry metric exporter** in Spring Boot (G-010-05). | Define an `SdkMeterProvider` bean (see [Operations](operations.md#opentelemetry)). |
| 10 | **A saga step cannot react to another saga's outcome event** (G-011-01): `SagaCompleted`, `SagaFailed` and `SagaCompensated` reach listeners, not sagas. | Listen in the application and publish a domain event, or send a command, that the follow-up saga starts on. |
| 11 | **A failed outbox command always compensates the whole saga**: no step can take the failure and name a business outcome (G-012-03), and a saga that already ended is not changed: a command that fails after its saga `COMPLETED` (G-012-02), or a compensation's command that fails after the saga `COMPENSATED` (G-012-01), only shows as a set-aside message and the warning `saga.command.failure.ignored`. | Send a command whose failure must stop the saga from a step the saga still waits after (it waits for the command's own reply event). Alert on `saga.command.failure.ignored` and on set-aside messages, and make compensation commands idempotent so redelivering one is safe. |

Further constraints of the model:

- **jMolecules domains** (see [Vocabularies](vocabularies.md)): an outbox command still needs Saga Forge's
  `@Command(delivery = OUTBOX)` beside jMolecules' `@Command` (G-016-01); a fixture test sees no Spring-published
  events, so a Spring Data aggregate's `@DomainEvents` need an event source registered in the test (G-016-02); a
  plain-typed identifier (`String`, `UUID`) on an event or command is never a link, mark it `@Association` (G-016-05);
  the in-memory transport keys an event linked only by identifier type by that type's name rather than the
  aggregate's, which still orders one aggregate's events together (G-016-06).

- **`SagaContext` values must be JSON scalars on Postgres** (`String`, `Boolean`, `Integer`, `Long`, finite `Double`,
  `List`, `Map` with `String` keys). Store `BigDecimal` as a string; a small `Long` reads back as `Integer` (G-003-07).
- **`SagaContext` values survive rollbacks and retries**: write them so that writing again is harmless.
- **Outside effects are not rolled back**: any handler that calls an outside system takes a `CommandId` parameter and
  passes `commandId.value()` on as the idempotency key (G-005-03). The triggering request itself is not deduplicated
  before a saga exists (G-005-04).
- **Compensation**: no wait for an undo's confirmation event (G-006-02); a stalled `COMPENSATING` instance resumes only
  through a recovery sweep after `saga-forge.recovery.stall-age`; a compensation sees the trigger's event type, not the event (G-006-06) — keep what it needs
  in `SagaContext`; a failed compensation is not retried on its own (G-006-09), only by an operator's resume, after which the instance keeps only the latest round's failure and earlier ones live in the history (G-015-03); compensations can run again after a crash, so
  their commands must be idempotent.
- **An unmarked exception ends the saga `FAILED` without compensation**; mark exceptions `TransientFailure` or
  `FinalFailure` (or list them in `retryOn`) when the difference matters.
- **An outbox command's failure is retried with the transport's backoff**, not the sending step's `@RetryPolicy`; an
  unmarked exception there is retried up to `saga-forge.transport.max-attempts` and then compensates the saga.
- **Publishing**: an application that publishes the same event both through Spring's `ApplicationEventPublisher` and
  through `EventPublisher` has it stored twice; keep one call. `saga-forge.application-events.mode=after-delivery` is
  deprecated and refused while the inbound route (`saga-forge.application-events.inbound.enabled`) is on. A
  hand-assembled runtime with the default `ImmediateDispatchOutbox` reports `DUPLICATE` for its own instance when a
  recorded event fans out to another saga type (G-014-04); so does any `EventReceiver` decorator that does not
  forward `receive(event, sourceSagaId)`.
- **Deadlines**: a deadline the relay already leased when it was cancelled is still delivered, then ignored
  (G-017-05); a scheduled command is not cancelled when its saga ends, so cancel it in the ending step if it must not
  run (G-017-06).
- **Operations**: every application instance runs recovery sweeps, each repair guarded by the instance's lock, not
  by leadership (G-015-02); an instance listing is read page by page, not as one snapshot, so an instance that changes
  between two pages may appear on both or neither (G-015-06).
- **Delivery order is per aggregate, not per saga instance** (G-007-04); the transport is at least once.
- **Not available**: Kafka transport, MySQL and MongoDB storage, a Quarkus extension, programmatic abort, Spring test
  slices for the fixture (G-009-01).
